title: GOOD: Geometry-Guided Out-of-Distribution Modeling
one_liner: When a point cloud segmentation model encounters new, unseen object classes in a new environment, cluster the points into superpoints and check their shape to tell which ones are unknown.
lead: A 3D point cloud is a dense set of coordinates describing the shape and structure of a real scene. When you train a segmentation model in one environment (say, a synthetic 3D world) and deploy it in a real one (a street with real traffic), the model encounters new classes it was never trained to recognize. The problem: there are far more known points than unknown ones, making it hard to spot what you should say "I don't know" about. GOOD fixes this by clustering nearby points together into compact chunks (superpoints), then confidently separating known from unknown chunks using their actual shape.

problem.h2: Known classes dominate; unknown ones hide in the noise
paras: A point cloud segmentation model learns to label points: road, car, tree, pedestrian. When you train it on synthetic data, the model sees equal numbers of each class. But when you deploy it to a real street, the distribution shifts: you still see mostly cars and roads (known classes), but now there are also new metal bollards and digital screens (unknown classes) scattered sparsely through the scene.

A beginner tries to add a confidence threshold: if the model's confidence is below 50%, call it unknown. This fails because the model is trained on known classes only. It assigns high confidence even to unfamiliar objects, simply because it is forced to pick one of the classes it knows. With 99% of the points being roads and cars anyway, even a perfect detector of unknown points gets drowned out by false positives.

callout.html: GOOD groups points by shape, then checks if a group's features match what the model learned during training.

steps.text: Group nearby points into compact chunks using geometric proximity and surface curvature.
For each superpoint, check if its features match patterns from the known classes.

steps.b: Threshold on shape, not raw score
steps.text: Points in low-confidence clusters are flagged as unknown, even if individual confidence scores are high.
Build and maintain memory of what known and unknown clusters look like over time.

steps.b: Online adaptation on known classes only
steps.text: Nudge the model to improve on known points; freeze behavior on unknown ones.

paras: GOOD changes how the model decides which points to learn from during deployment. Instead of using per-point confidence scores (which are unreliable when classes are unfamiliar), it groups points into shape-aware chunks and makes the known-vs-unknown decision at the cluster level. This shift from individual point scores to shape-aware group decisions is the core move.

hidden.h2: Cluster confidence: knowing when a group is unknown
hidden.name: Cluster confidence score
paras: Cluster confidence is a single number per superpoint that estimates how likely that chunk of points belongs to a class the model has seen before. It is not the same as the average of individual point confidences. Instead, it looks at the whole group's geometric shape, local density, and feature distribution — asking: does this cluster match the signature of known classes or does it look alien?

The paper estimates it by checking: do the features of this cluster's points align with the prototype representations (learned memory of known classes) or do they diverge? If they diverge far enough, the cluster is flagged as unknown.

heat.caption: Darker means the cluster is confidently known. Light clusters are unknown or uncertain.

reads.html: A cluster is confident if its points form a tight group with features that match what you learned during training.
Cluster confidence is derived from the distance between the cluster's feature centroid and the nearest prototype, scaled by the cluster's compactness and size.

mechanism.h2: Why shape alone can separate known from unknown
paras: During training on synthetic data, the model learns: what does a road cluster look like? (flat, large, low curvature). What does a car look like? (compact, curved edges, higher density). These become mental templates, or prototypes, in the model's memory.

When a new object appears (a real-world bollard), it is sparse and has a different curvature signature than anything in training. If you only used per-point confidence, the model would guess "car" or "road" because those are the only choices it knows. But if you ask: does this cluster match any of my learned templates? — the answer is no. The shape alone reveals the unknown, without needing to know what the bollard is called.

The mechanism is simple: train the model to memorize the shape of known classes as prototypes. At test time, cluster incoming points and ask: are these points geometrically similar to any learned cluster shape? If not, do not learn from them. If yes, adapt. This works because unfamiliar objects have unfamiliar shapes, even if the model would confuse them if forced to classify.

stages.s: Group into superpoints by spatial proximity

math.words: Cluster confidence is the minimum distance from the cluster centroid to any known prototype, divided by cluster compactness, minus a bias term.
symbols: confidence score for cluster c (higher = more known)
average feature vector of all points in cluster c
prototype feature vector for known class p
distance (how far apart the two feature vectors are)
smallest distance across all known prototypes
weight controlling how much cluster shape matters
how tightly packed the points in cluster c are (higher = more compact)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Cluster A (known road): features at [0.2, 0.1], nearest prototype road at [0.25, 0.15]. Distance = 0.07. Compactness = 0.9 (tight). Confidence = -0.07 + 0.8 * 0.9 = 0.65 (confident known).
Cluster B (unknown bollard): features at [0.5, 0.8], nearest prototype car at [0.3, 0.2]. Distance = 0.42. Compactness = 0.4 (loose). Confidence = -0.42 + 0.8 * 0.4 = -0.10 (flagged unknown).
Same shape-based reasoning: tight clusters near learned shapes score high; loose clusters far from everything score low.

math.note: Higher confidence means the cluster resembles something the model learned; lower confidence means it looks alien and should not be used for learning.

bars.h2: Before and after: handling unknown objects

charts.title: Naive per-point confidence (fails)
charts.note: Unknown objects are assigned high confidence, corrupting the adaptation.

charts.title: GOOD with cluster confidence (works)
charts.note: Cluster shape separates unknown objects even when per-point confidence is high.

items.html: If unknown objects form very large or very dense clusters, they may match known prototypes by accident. A large bollard field might look like a road to the clustering algorithm.
If the model adapts and the prototypes drift over time, old learned shapes may no longer match new scenes, triggering false unknown labels.
If known classes have high internal variation (cars are many shapes), a single prototype per class may miss some instances, treating valid known points as unknown.
Maintain fresh prototypes, use geometric diversity in training, and validate on scenes with many unknown object shapes before deployment.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Implement GOOD on synthetic-to-real segmentation: train on Synth4D (3D synthetic city), deploy on real SemanticKITTI footage (real driving scenes). Cluster the test point cloud into superpoints. Extract features and compare to learned prototypes. Measure: (1) how many unknown points are correctly flagged, (2) how much the model accuracy on known classes improves during adaptation, (3) how few known points are mistakenly rejected as unknown.
demo.closing: If the demo shows higher rejection of unknown objects AND lower corruption of known class accuracy compared to per-point confidence thresholds, the geometric separation is real.
